opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my first reaction was skepticism, and I think that's the healthy reaction. For years the standard workflow in enterprise machine learning has been: you have a relational database with many tables, customers, transactions, products, and you spend weeks or months doing feature engineering, joining tables, building aggregates, and then training a task-specific model for each prediction problem. Churn is one model, fraud is another, recommendations are a third. So the idea that you could skip all of that and have one pretrained model that just looks at the database and answers a predictive query sounds almost too good to be true.

What changed my mind was thinking about the database the right way. If you view a relational database not as a collection of flat tables but as a graph, where rows are nodes and primary-foreign key relationships are edges, then a lot of what feature engineering does is really message passing done by hand. People manually compute "number of purchases in the last 30 days" or "average order value of this user's friends." A graph neural network, or a graph transformer, can learn those patterns directly from the structure.

The second piece is in-context learning. We've seen with large language models that a pretrained model can adapt to a new task from examples placed in its context, without updating weights. The question was whether that works for structured, relational data. And the key insight is that for a given prediction task, the database itself provides the in-context examples. If you want to predict whether a customer will churn next month, you can go back in time and sample historical customers where you already know the outcome. Those labeled subgraphs become the context, and the model makes a prediction for the new entity in a single forward pass.

So my reaction evolved from "this can't work" to "this is surprising but it makes sense," and then, as we saw the results, to genuine excitement. In many cases you get predictions in seconds that are competitive with, and sometimes better than, models that data scientists spent a long time building. And if you do need extra accuracy, you can still fine-tune on the specific task.

I'll also be honest about the limits. It doesn't mean that domain expertise goes away, and it doesn't mean every single task is solved out of the box. Data quality still matters, defining the right prediction question still matters. But I think it fundamentally changes where people spend their time: less on plumbing and feature pipelines, more on asking the right questions of their data. That's the shift I find most exciting.

r001.rationale: The speaker says the idea first seemed too good to be true, and even after seeing results calls it “surprising but it makes sense,” conveying that it still surprises them that it works.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, because honestly, I'll admit that when we first started down this road, I was skeptical of the claim myself. You have to remember where we were coming from. The entire history of machine learning on tabular and relational data has been this extremely manual, bespoke process. A data scientist sits down with a database, they figure out what they're predicting, they spend weeks or months doing feature engineering, joining tables, aggregating things, and then they train a model that is specific to that one task on that one database. If the schema changes, if the task changes, you start over. So the idea that you could have one network, trained once, that you never update, and you just point it at a database it has never seen, with a schema it has never seen, and it gives you a prediction in one forward pass, that sounds almost too good to be true. It sounds like the kind of thing you'd put on a slide to raise money.

What changed my mind was really two things. The first was conceptual. When we started thinking about relational deep learning, the insight was that a relational database is already a graph. The foreign key, primary key relationships are edges. The tables are node types. The rows are nodes. And once you see it that way, you realize that a lot of what feature engineering was doing by hand, the aggregations and the joins, is exactly what message passing in a graph neural network does automatically. So the structure was already there. The second piece was borrowing the lesson from language models, which is that if you pretrain on enough diverse data, you get representations that transfer. And the analogy I like is that in language we went from training a separate model for sentiment, a separate model for translation, a separate model for question answering, to one model that does all of it through in-context learning. The question we asked was, why can't databases work the same way?

So when we actually built this, the relational foundation model, and we saw that you could take a frozen model, give it a few labeled examples in context, and it would match or beat task-specific models that had been trained with weeks of engineering, that is when my reaction went from skepticism to, okay, this is real. And now I'd say my reaction has evolved one step further, to thinking about what it means for how people use data. Because the bottleneck was never the model, really. The bottleneck was the human time to build a model per question. If predictions become something you just query, the way you query the database itself, then the number of questions an organization can ask goes up by orders of magnitude. That is the part I find exciting now. Not the single forward pass as a technical trick, but what it unlocks.

r001.rationale: The response describes initial skepticism and later accepting that the model works, but it does not say the speaker remains surprised that it works.

astra-6.text:
My first reaction was skepticism. You’re saying that you can take a pretrained neural network, freeze its weights, give it a database it has never seen before, and make useful predictions with a forward pass? That challenges how we usually think about machine learning, where you collect data for a particular task and then train a model specifically for it.

But the idea becomes less mysterious when you think about what happens during that forward pass. Frozen weights don’t mean the prediction is independent of the data you provide. The model can use that data as context and infer patterns without updating its parameters.

So I’ve moved from asking, “Can this possibly work?” to asking, “Under what conditions does it work?” How well does it generalize to a genuinely different database? What information does it need in context? And how does it compare with a model trained for that particular task? That’s where the interesting questions are.

r001.rationale: The response describes initial skepticism and then says the idea becomes “less mysterious,” but it does not clearly convey that the speaker remains surprised that it actually works.

sol-6.1.text:
My first reaction was skepticism. If you freeze the model, how can it make useful predictions on a database it has never seen before? You would expect to train something specifically for that database and that prediction task.

But the key is that frozen weights don’t mean the model has no information about the new task. You can give it examples and context as input. So the question becomes whether it has learned a sufficiently general procedure for using that context to make a prediction.

I’ve become more open to that possibility. I would still distinguish between showing that it works on a benchmark and showing that it works reliably across real databases. What information goes into that forward pass? How much preparation is required? And how does it compare with a model trained for the task? Those are the questions that would determine how excited I’d be.

r001.rationale: The response describes initial skepticism and later openness, but does not clearly say the speaker remains surprised that the approach actually works.
